transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samir Chen (Redwood SE), Taylor Wong (Redwood CSM); Lena Ortiz (Comet CTO), Marco Ruiz (Lead Eng), Nina Park (Sec)
summary: Quick SDK walkthrough (Python + TypeScript) covering auth/env setup, quickstarts, and next steps for a pilot and security review. Customer wants low-latency hosted API for payment risk scoring but needs answers on data residency, KMS, and SSO for onboarding.
topics: SDK quickstart (pip / npm) and example app
Auth: API keys vs SSO/OIDC, env vars, KMS for encryption
Environment setup: staging vs prod, VPC/private deployment considerations
Performance hints: batching, prefix caching, token limits
full_transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really appreciate you making the time. Quick intro, I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE on the account. Samir our solutions engineer is here to walk through SDKs and a quick integration.
[00:10] Lena: Hi yes thanks, Lena here. We run risk scoring for transactions, pretty sensitive data so Nina's on for security questions.
[00:18] Marco: Marco, lead eng. We're most interested in Python and TypeScript examples so we can drop them into our microservices.
[00:27] Samir: Great, that's exactly what we'll cover. We'll do a short run through the Python quickstart, then TypeScript, then auth patterns and env setup.
[01:05] Jordan: Quick low-level context, Comet is evaluating hosted Redwood API for latency but wants to understand Dedicated and Private options for compliance. We'll keep that in mind.
[02:02] Samir: Ok jumping into a screen share, so on the repo side we have two quickstarts: /quickstarts/python and /quickstarts/ts. For Python it's as simple as pip install redwood-sdk, set REDWOOD_API_KEY as env var and you're up. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-... then python app.py.
[02:45] Marco: Real quick, are the keys scoped per project or per user? We have a multi-tenant internal platform.
[02:52] Samir: Keys are project-scoped by default, you can create service tokens with limited scopes. We also support SSO/OIDC for user-level auth when you run Private with your IdP.
[03:30] Nina: For Private — how does KMS work? We need customer-managed keys for encryption at rest.
[03:39] Samir: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS). For hosted, we offer envelope encryption and can integrate with your KMS under an enterprise agreement.
[04:10] Jordan: A note — housekeeping: in the transcript sometimes our product names get munged by auto-transcribe; e.g., Redwood Dedicated sometimes comes out as "Redwood dedicade". Ignore that.
[04:40] Samir: Back to SDKs. Python quickstart shows a basic call to client.generate(...) for scoring. We pass a prompt with transaction context. Example snippet pasted in chat.
[05:22] Samir: On the TypeScript side, npm i @redwood/inference, then set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or use a .env file with dotenv. Example: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[06:05] Marco: Any idempotency patterns recommended when sending scoring requests? We do retries and want to avoid double scoring.
[06:20] Samir: We recommend idempotency keys per transaction. Also, for throughput, do batching: the SDK supports .batchPredict and we have a built-in prefix/K-V cache that reduces repeated token costs — sometimes transcribed as "K-V cash" in notes.
[07:15] Jordan: Can we talk about environmental separation? Staging vs prod, and how keys rotate?
[07:28] Samir: Typical pattern: separate projects in Redwood, separate API keys for staging/prod, rotate keys via the console or API. We also support short-lived service tokens if you want automatic rotation.
[08:05] Lena: Ok looks good. For our compliance team, they need audit logs and retention controls — can you confirm?
[08:22] Samir: Yes — Console provides per-request logs with token-level cost and latency metadata, and enterprise plans can extend retention and export logs to S3. We also have audit events for model changes and route changes.
[09:00] Nina: About data residency — Comet needs EU residency for EU customers. What are options with hosted?
[09:12] Samir: Hosted supports region pinning — requests can be routed to eu-west-1 nodes; for stricter requirements, Private VPC/on-prem ensures data never leaves customer network.
[09:50] Marco: Back to SDK examples — error handling patterns? We see 429s occasionally in other vendors, how do you suggest handling backoff?
[10:03] Samir: Exponential backoff with jitter. The SDK exposes rate limit headers; you can catch 429 and look at Retry-After. For sustained traffic, Dedicated clusters give predictable throughput; Redwood will route to Dedicated if you purchase reserved capacity.
[11:00] Jordan: Quick objection we hear: latency vs cost — customers often want low latency but are concerned about unit costs. Any guidance?
[11:12] Samir: Tradeoffs: lower latency often means smaller batching and more expensive per-token cost. We recommend intelligent batching with per-route SLOs. Redwood Optimize gives batching suggestions and quantization profiles to lower cost while hitting latency targets.
[12:05] Marco: Can you demo a real quick run of the TypeScript quickstart hitting the hosted endpoint?
[12:15] Samir: Sure, running the demo... (background typing)
[13:00] Samir: Ok running: node quickstarts/ts/demo.js — it shows the request and streamed tokens back. Note: streaming works out-of-the-box; you can hook into the onToken callback.
[13:40] Marco: The transcript shows a small glitch — sometimes the stream label is off, but we see the payload.
[14:05] Samir: For local envs, we recommend using a .env file with the REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_ENV=staging. For Docker, pass envs or use secrets manager.
[15:00] Lena: How about CI — do you recommend passing real keys into CI?
[15:08] Samir: Use short-lived tokens and secrets manager integration. Don't store long-lived keys in repo. We also have IP allow-listing for service tokens.
[16:00] Jordan: Security doc follow up — Samir will share the SOC 2 appendix and KMS pattern.
[16:12] Samir: Yep will share the packet after this call.
[17:00] Marco: A couple technical Qs: what's the recommended max sequence length and how does the KV cache behave?
[17:15] Samir: Typical models support 2k-16k tokens; KV cache means repeated prefixes are cached server-side, reduces recomputation. For scoring, keep prompts concise. The runtime compiles kernels and selects optimized paths based on seq len, sometimes called kernel selection.
[18:00] Nina: For Private deployment, how does networking look? We have strict egress policies.
[18:10] Samir: Private can run inside your VPC with customer-managed control plane. You can opt-in to air-gapped installs; there are additional setup steps and lead time.
[19:05] Marco: For performance testing, would you provide a sample harness?
[19:12] Samir: Yes, we'll share a small benchmark harness and a runbook. It will include sample payloads, concurrency settings and a suggested instance spec.
[20:00] (short pause)
[20:10] Jordan: Quick alignment — Comet's success criteria are: 1) <100ms p50 inference for single-score path, 2) cost per 1k transactions below threshold, 3) SOC2 paperwork complete. Confirm?
[20:24] Lena: Yes. Those are the metrics.
[21:00] Samir: Let me call out a code snippet for Python error handling: try/except around client.generate, check for .retriable flag, use backoff, and leverage client.batch for many items.
[22:00] Jordan: Are there existing integrations or connectors for event streaming? We use Kafka.
[22:12] Samir: Customers typically run a stateless worker that consumes Kafka, calls Redwood client, then stores results. The SDK is lightweight and supports async calls. We have a reference pattern in the quickstarts.
[23:00] Marco: Any gotchas with TypeScript types? We sometimes get mismatched payload shapes.
[23:08] Samir: The TS SDK includes type definitions; we recommend using the provided types and enabling strict mode. For structured outputs, specify response schema to reduce parsing errors.
[24:00] (background noise)
[24:30] Nina: On auditing — can we get per-tenant logs exported to our S3?
[24:45] Samir: Yes, enterprise plans support log export and custom retention. We'll include export configs in the security packet.
[25:30] Jordan: Let's hit quickstart commands so you have them in chat. Python: git clone repo, cd quickstarts/python, pip install -r requirements.txt, export REDWOOD_API_KEY=..., python app.py. TypeScript: cd quickstarts/ts, npm install, cp .env.example .env, set REDWOOD_API_KEY, npm run demo.
[26:40] Marco: Great. For the API payload, what fields should we send for scoring? Just transaction json and user history?
[26:55] Samir: Send a concise prompt with transaction metadata: amount, user_id, ip, device_fingerprint. We also support embeddings for user history if you want contextual signals.
[27:40] Marco: Is there a limit on concurrent requests per key?
[27:50] Samir: Default rate limits exist; for high concurrency we recommend Dedicated or reserved capacity. We'll surface limits in the console and via headers.
[28:30] Jordan: Competitors asked — do you evaluate Anthropic and OpenAI?
[28:38] Samir: Yes customers compare across all; Redwood's differentiation is production features like routing, caching, and cost controls.
[29:20] Lena: One more on SSO — can Redwood integrate with our Okta?
[29:28] Samir: Yes Okta via OIDC/SAML for Private and enterprise hosted SSO. We'll include setup steps.
[30:10] Marco: For deployment, if we go Private, how long is lead time?
[30:18] Samir: Depends on infra — VPC-based Private is typically 4-8 weeks; on-prem or air-gapped longer. We can scope during POC.
[31:00] Jordan: Ok quick recap and next steps. We'll send quickstarts, security docs, and benchmark harness. Comet will run smoke tests and share outputs.
[31:30] Lena: Good. Nina will evaluate the KMS and SSO sections next week.
[32:05] Marco: I'll create a ticket and paste results.
[33:00] Samir: Any remaining technical blockers?
[33:08] Marco: Not right now. We'll start with hosted in eu region as a baseline test.
[34:00] Jordan: Great — final notes on costs: we'll send an example pricing sheet for hosted vs Dedicated to show unit economics with batching.
[34:20] Samir: Also note Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles to lower cost for the same quality.
[35:12] Nina: We'd like to see a security SLA and pen test report.
[35:28] Samir: We'll include the pen test summary and SLA in the packet.
[36:00] (wrap up)
[36:20] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and schedule the benchmark session.
[36:35] Lena: Thanks all.
[36:40] Marco: Thanks.
[36:45] Nina: Bye.
[37:00] (call ends)

Notes: auto-transcription has occasional typos (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, "Redwood dedicade" for Redwood Dedicated). Shared links posted in chat: https://github.com/redwood/quickstarts (Python + TS), security packet link placeholder: https://redwood.example.com/security/comet-packet, benchmark harness: https://redwood.example.com/bench/comet-harness.
